senses.gloss:
eṣaṇātraya
(‘three desires’)
------------------------------------------
The उपनिषद्स्, the crowning glory of Hindu Philosophy, often stress the great importance of वैराग्य or renunciation. Though this is a negative aspect of sādhanā (spiritual discipline), it is of primary importance even as the cleaning of a cloth is necessary before it is coloured.
The principal aspect of this वैराग्य is eṣaṇātrayatyāga or renunciation of three types of yearnings which are serious impediments in the path of spiritual progress. The three desires—collectively known as एषणात्रय are: putraiṣaṇā (the desire for a son), vittaiṣaṇā (the desire for wealth) and lokaiṣaṇā (the desire to attain हेअवेन् after death) (vide Bṛhadā-raṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.5.1).
Since the first desire needs a wife for its fulfilment, it is also called ‘jāyaiṣaṇā’ or ‘dāraiṣaṇā’ (desire for a wife).
Putraiṣaṇā is aimed at discharging the debt called पितृ-ऋण, towards the forefathers, by the performance of obsequial rites like śrāddha. This will also prevent the person from going to हेल्ल् after death.
Vittaiṣaṇā helps one to perform the various वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस् by which one can get to हेअवेन्. This automatically satisfies lokaiṣaṇā also.
However, all these three continue to bind the जीव or the individual सोउल्, to सṁसार or transmigratory existence. Hence the need to give them up.
Medical treatises like those of चरक (1400 B. C.) replace putraiṣaṇā by prāṇaiṣaṇā (the desire to live) in which case it is a good desire and hence need not be given up.
